messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Abdul Rahman, a 78-year-old African American man who had worked for most of his life as a librarian, came to the clinic with his wife after years of trying to keep his distress private. He described the terrorist attack that had shattered his sense of safety as happening in a crowded civic building during a public event, when the normal sounds of conversation, movement, and anticipation were suddenly broken by chaos and violence. In his telling, the memory remained painfully exact: the layout of the room, the faces, the sounds, the immediate fear on people’s faces. He said the scene could return to him “like a film,” and that he could be walking through the quiet aisles of the library or sitting at home and, without warning, feel the whole thing come back in full detail. What startled him most was how often it arrived tied to ordinary moments that should have been harmless. A remark on the radio, a discussion about current affairs, or even hearing people speak carelessly about cruelty or disrespect could pull him straight back into that moment, because what disturbed him most was not only the danger but the moral violation of it all. People “misbehaving,” as he put it, had become intolerable to him, as if disorder and selfishness were the first signs that the world could again tip into catastrophe.

Over time, Abdul’s vivid and replaying memory began shaping the way he moved through daily life. He started avoiding things that might make him feel briefly hopeful or glad, because happiness felt to him almost reckless, like lowering his guard. He found himself drifting off into a world of his own in the middle of conversations, letting his mind slip away from the present whenever the surroundings felt emotionally loaded or too open. At the library, he would take longer routes through the building, choose quieter tasks, and keep his attention fixed on books and catalogues rather than on people. Crowds became especially difficult. Shopping centres, community events, and even larger gatherings connected with his church were places he began to pass up, because the density of people, the noise, and the sense that anything could happen at once made him feel cornered. His wife noticed that on the anniversary of the attack he became more withdrawn and irritable, sometimes refusing even planned family outings. Those dates brought the memory back more sharply, and the stronger the memory grew, the more he pulled away from anything that might stir feelings, conversation, or company. He had come to believe that if he allowed himself pleasure, or if he stayed too long among people and noise, he would be less prepared for another terrible breach.

Yet the very habits that seemed to keep him safe had also made the memory more dominant. When Abdul shut down hopeful moments and retreated into his own private world, the attack returned with greater force and less interruption, as if his mind had fewer places to go than back to the scene itself. The film-like replay became easier to trigger in part because he was constantly scanning for the kinds of things that might set it off: rude behaviour, heated topics, anniversaries, crowded spaces. That watching made the world feel full of danger, and because he was so alert for it, small moments could suddenly ignite the full memory without warning. A stranger speaking sharply in the supermarket, a news discussion at the library about violence, or someone behaving thoughtlessly in a queue could all seize him in an instant. Once that happened, the old scene was vivid again, and he would avoid the rest of the day, withdraw from conversation, or escape into reverie just to get through it. In that way, the memory and the avoidance had begun to feed each other, each making the other harder to escape.

By the time he sought help, Abdul’s world had narrowed considerably. He was still going to work less reliably than before, and his wife had begun to worry about how much of his day he spent disconnected and how often he refused invitations that might have brought him comfort. He did not come because he thought himself weak; he came because the pattern was tightening, and he feared that the anniversary, the wrong conversation, or an ordinary encounter with people behaving badly would once again pull him helplessly into the same full and detailed horror. What he most hoped for was some way to live without bracing himself against every hint of joy or danger, and what frightened him most was that the memory would keep claiming his present until there was little of it left.
